overview.title: Text-to-image diffusion and Stable Diffusion in KerasHub
overview.main_topic: How a diffusion model becomes a text-to-image model by conditioning the denoiser on embeddings from a pretrained text encoder, and loading the pretrained Stable Diffusion 3 model from KerasHub.
overview.central_idea: Train the same denoising diffusion process on (prompt, image) pairs and feed the denoiser text embeddings alongside the noisy images. At inference you can denoise pure noise toward an image that matches a new prompt. Instead of training such a model, the book loads Stable Diffusion 3 Medium with `keras_hub.models.TextToImage.from_preset`.
overview.importance: This page connects the from-scratch flower generator to production text-to-image systems. Conceptually, only one thing changes: the denoiser gets a second input. In practice, KerasHub gives access to a state-of-the-art pretrained model in a few lines.
learning_objectives: Describe the two inputs of a text-conditioned denoiser (noisy_images and text_embeddings) and the role of a pretrained text encoder.
Explain why text conditioning makes denoising easier and enables prompting with never-before-seen text.
Explain why the book uses a pretrained model rather than training a text-to-image model.
Read Listing 17.8 and say what TextToImage.from_preset, the preset name and image_shape do.
prerequisites: Diffusion models and the denoising loop (pp.542–554)
KerasHub presets (used for LLMs in chapter 16)

summary:
Section 17.3 extends the diffusion model of section 17.2 to **text-to-image generation**. The recipe has two parts:

1. A **pretrained text encoder**, such as a Transformer encoder like RoBERTa from chapter 15, maps a text prompt to vectors in a continuous embedding space.
2. A diffusion model is trained on **`(prompt, image)` pairs**, where each prompt is a short description of its image.

Images are handled as before: the model learns to map noisy input to a denoised output that progressively approaches the image. The key change is that the embedded prompt is also passed to the denoiser, so it takes two inputs, `noisy_images` and `text_embeddings`. This makes the job easier than for the flower denoiser. Instead of removing noise with no other information, the model gets a textual description of the final image to guide denoising.

After training, you can start from pure noise, supply a **never-before-seen prompt**, and denoise into an image for that prompt, because the model maps noise to images *conditioned on* a text representation.

The authors do not train such a model, because doing it well is expensive and slow. Instead they use **Stable Diffusion**, a pretrained model in KerasHub made by Stability AI, a company that builds open image and video generation models. Figure 17.13 shows an output: an astronaut riding a blue origami elephant on a New York street. **Listing 17.8** begins with `import keras_hub`, sets `height, width = 512, 512`, and calls `keras_hub.models.TextToImage.from_preset("stable_diffusion_3_medium", image_shape=(height, width, 3), ...)`. The call continues on p.556 with `dtype="float16"`, then defines the prompt and calls `task.generate(prompt)`.

paragraphs.excerpt: We can use the same basic diffusion process to create a model
paragraphs.what_it_says: The same diffusion process can map text to images. You need a pretrained text encoder (such as a RoBERTa-like Transformer encoder from chapter 15) that maps text to vectors in a continuous embedding space, and then you train a diffusion model on (prompt, image) pairs, where each prompt is a short description of the image.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The text encoder is not trained from scratch with the diffusion model. It is reused from language modeling, where it has already learned to map semantically similar texts to nearby vectors. The diffusion model only has to learn how to use those vectors. The dataset changes from unlabeled images (Oxford Flowers) to captioned images. The caption plays a role similar to a label in supervised learning, but it is free-form text rather than a class index.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the recipe behind systems such as Stable Diffusion, DALL·E and Imagen. Because the text side is pretrained, the image model inherits the encoder's understanding of language, including generalization to word combinations never seen together in training.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: Stable Diffusion 3 actually uses three pretrained text encoders (two CLIP text encoders and, optionally, T5-XXL). This explains the 4,096-dim sequence and 2,048-dim pooled embeddings you will see on p.558. CLIP encoders are trained contrastively against images, which makes their embeddings especially well aligned with visual content.

terminology.meaning: A network, already trained on text, that maps a token sequence to vectors; here it is frozen and used to embed prompts.
The training data of a text-to-image model: images with short captions describing them.
A vector space in which texts are points and similar meanings are near each other, so you can move smoothly between them (see p.557).

connections: p.554: the previous page announced text conditioning as the next step.
p.557: the continuity of the text embedding space is exploited for latent-space walks.

paragraphs.excerpt: We can handle the image input in the same way as we
paragraphs.what_it_says: The image side works as before: noisy input is mapped to a denoised output that approaches the image. The difference is that the embedded prompt is also passed to the denoiser, which therefore takes two inputs, noisy_images and text_embeddings. This gives it an advantage over the flower denoiser, because the textual representation of the final image guides the denoising. After training, pure noise plus a never-before-seen prompt can be denoised into an image for that prompt. The book will not train such a model (it is expensive and slow) and instead uses the pretrained Stable Diffusion in KerasHub, made by Stability AI. Its third version can be used with a couple of lines of code (figure 17.13). The last words of this sentence ('Hub with just a couple of lines of code', e07) appear below the figure.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Conditioning reduces uncertainty. At high noise levels an unconditional denoiser has to guess what image is hidden in the noise, and its prediction is a blurry average over all plausible images. With the caption, the set of plausible images shrinks, so predictions are sharper and generation is steered toward the prompt. Because the encoder maps any text to the embedding space, the model can be given prompts never seen during training. It responds to where the prompt lands in embedding space, which is how compositions like 'astronaut riding an origami elephant' become possible. Note that the flower denoiser actually took two inputs too, `[noisy_images, noise_rates]` (p.550). So the text-conditioned denoiser has the noisy images, the noise level and the text embeddings; the book simplifies this to 'two inputs'.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This explains why text-to-image models generalize. They do not retrieve images for prompts; they denoise under the guidance of a continuous text representation. It also motivates using pretrained models: training a good text-to-image model needs hundreds of millions of captioned images and very large compute budgets.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): Stable Diffusion 3 is a latent diffusion model. Denoising runs in the compressed latent space of an image autoencoder (64×64×16 for a 512×512 image, as Listing 17.9 on p.558 shows), and its denoiser is a Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT) rather than a U-Net. Text and image tokens interact through joint attention.

terminology.meaning: The two (named) inputs the book gives the text-conditioned denoiser: the noised image batch and the encoded prompt.
Producing outputs whose distribution depends on a given input, here a vector representation of text.
A family of open text-to-image diffusion models by Stability AI; the book uses version 3 (medium) via KerasHub.
Keras's library of pretrained models and tasks, loaded through presets.

connections: p.550: the flower denoiser takes [noisy_images, noise_rates] and predicts noise masks.
p.544: a diffusion model is 'a denoising autoencoder in a loop'.
p.557: the 'medium' model is the smallest SD3 variant (about 3 billion parameters).

concepts.name: Text-conditioned diffusion
concepts.definition: A diffusion model whose denoiser receives text embeddings of a prompt in addition to the noisy image, so that generation is steered toward images matching the prompt.
concepts.intuition: Restoring a badly damaged photo is much easier if someone tells you what it shows.
concepts.technical: Training data: (prompt, image) pairs. The denoiser predicts noise from (noisy image, noise level, text embedding). Inference: start from Gaussian noise, fix the prompt embedding, run the denoising loop.
concepts.significance: This is the mechanism behind modern text-to-image generation.
concepts.example: Figure 17.13: the prompt about an astronaut on an origami elephant produces a matching image.
concepts.misconception: The model does not look up images matching words. It produces a new image by denoising, guided by an embedding.

concepts.name: Pretrained text encoder
concepts.definition: A Transformer encoder (the book suggests something like RoBERTa) that maps text to vectors in a continuous embedding space.
concepts.intuition: A translator that turns words into coordinates the image model can understand.
concepts.technical: The prompt is tokenized and passed through the encoder. Its token-level outputs (a sequence) and/or a pooled vector are given to the denoiser. SD3 passes both (pp.558–559).
concepts.significance: Reusing a pretrained encoder lets the image model benefit from language understanding learned elsewhere.
concepts.example: RoBERTa from chapter 15; in SD3, CLIP and T5 encoders (beyond the book).
concepts.misconception: The text encoder does not generate images; it only provides the conditioning signal.

concepts.name: Stable Diffusion (KerasHub TextToImage)
concepts.definition: A pretrained open text-to-image diffusion model from Stability AI, available in KerasHub as a TextToImage task preset.
concepts.intuition: A ready-made version of the text-conditioned denoiser described on this page, trained at scale.
concepts.technical: Loaded with keras_hub.models.TextToImage.from_preset("stable_diffusion_3_medium", image_shape=(512, 512, 3), dtype="float16"). The task bundles preprocessor (tokenizers), backbone (text encoders, diffusion transformer, VAE) and the generate() loop.
concepts.significance: Lets readers experiment with state-of-the-art text-to-image generation without training anything.
concepts.example: task.generate("A NASA astraunaut riding an origami elephant in New York City") on p.556.
concepts.misconception: Loading the preset does not train or fine-tune anything; it downloads fixed pretrained weights.

code.title: Creating a Stable Diffusion text-to-image model (first part)
code.original_code:
import keras_hub
height, width = 512, 512
task = keras_hub.models.TextToImage.from_preset(
    "stable_diffusion_3_medium",
    image_shape=(height, width, 3),
code.what_it_does: Imports KerasHub, fixes the output resolution at 512×512, and starts building a high-level TextToImage task from the 'stable_diffusion_3_medium' preset with RGB images of shape (512, 512, 3). The call is completed on p.556 with dtype="float16".

line_explanations.explanation: KerasHub is the Keras library of pretrained models; it was used for LLMs in chapter 16.
Output resolution. The latent noise in Listing 17.9 (p.558) has spatial size height // 8 by width // 8 (64×64), because the image autoencoder downsamples by 8.
TextToImage.from_preset builds the task (preprocessor plus backbone) and downloads the preset's weights.
The preset name: Stable Diffusion 3, 'medium' size, the smallest SD3 release (about 3 billion parameters, p.557).
image_shape sets the resolution the model generates: height, width and 3 color channels.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: the preset name and configuration. Output: a `task` object with a `generate()` method that maps a prompt (or a dict with prompts and negative prompts) to a uint8 image array.
code.algorithm: Instantiate tokenizers, text encoders, diffusion backbone and image decoder from the preset config; load pretrained weights; wrap them in a task with generation logic.
code.theory_link: This is the text-conditioned diffusion model described in the page text, pretrained by Stability AI rather than trained in the book.

parameters.name: "stable_diffusion_3_medium"
parameters.role: Which pretrained configuration and weights to download.

parameters.name: image_shape
parameters.role: Resolution (and channels) of generated images; (512, 512, 3) here.

pitfalls: The listing is incomplete on this page; the dtype="float16" argument and closing parenthesis are on p.556. Without half precision the model may not fit in a free Colab GPU's memory.
The SD3 weights are large and may require accepting Stability AI's license on the hosting hub (e.g., Kaggle/Hugging Face) before download (beyond the book).

deeper.title: Why the caption makes denoising easier
deeper.body:
1. At high noise, an image is almost pure Gaussian noise. An unconditional denoiser trained with an averaging loss predicts something close to the *average* of all images consistent with the noise, which is blurry.
2. Adding the caption $c$ changes the target from $\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t]$ to $\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t, c]$. The set of plausible clean images is much smaller, so the prediction is sharper and pointed in a meaningful direction.
3. Repeating this at each step drives the trajectory from noise toward an image consistent with the caption.
4. Because $c$ comes from a continuous text embedding, prompts never seen in training still land somewhere meaningful, and the model interpolates (pp.557–560).

This is an expectation-based view (an AI explanation); the book says the same thing qualitatively.

deeper.title: Restoring a photo with and without a caption
deeper.body: Imagine restoring a heavily water-damaged photograph. Alone, you can tell there is something reddish in the middle. If someone hands you a note saying 'red tulips in a vase on a windowsill', every smudge becomes easier to interpret. The flower model works without the note; the text-to-image model always has one.

misconceptions.claim: A text-to-image model needs a completely different algorithm from the unconditional diffusion model.
misconceptions.correction: The denoising process is the same. The denoiser gets an extra input (text embeddings) and is trained on (prompt, image) pairs.

misconceptions.claim: The model can only draw prompts it saw during training.
misconceptions.correction: Because the prompt is mapped to a continuous embedding space, new prompts land in meaningful places and the model can denoise toward them.

misconceptions.claim: The text encoder is trained together with the image model from scratch.
misconceptions.correction: The book uses a pretrained text encoder, which maps text to vectors before diffusion training begins.

takeaways: A text-to-image diffusion model is the same diffusion process with a denoiser that also receives text embeddings from a pretrained text encoder.
It is trained on (prompt, image) pairs; at inference, noise plus a new prompt is denoised into a matching image.
The text provides guidance that makes denoising easier than in the unconditional flower model.
Training such a model well is expensive, so the book uses the pretrained Stable Diffusion 3 (medium) from KerasHub via TextToImage.from_preset.

questions.question: What two inputs does the book say the text-conditioned denoising model takes?
questions.explanation: The page says the model takes `noisy_images` and `text_embeddings`. Class labels (option 1) would be class conditioning, not text. Clean images are the target, not an input at inference (option 3). Discriminators belong to GANs (option 4).

questions.question: What training data does a text-to-image diffusion model need, according to the page?
questions.answer: (prompt, image) pairs, where each prompt is a short textual description of its image.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the first paragraph of section 17.3.

questions.question: Why does conditioning on text 'give a leg up' compared with the unconditional flower denoiser?
questions.answer: The denoiser gets a textual representation of the final image, so it no longer has to infer what image is hidden in the noise from the noise alone. The space of plausible outputs shrinks and denoising is guided toward the described image.
questions.explanation: The book: 'Instead of learning to remove noise from an image without any additional information, the model gets to use a textual representation of the final image to help guide the denoising process.'

questions.question: Why does the book use a pretrained Stable Diffusion model instead of training a text-to-image model itself?
options: Training one that works well is expensive and time consuming
Text-to-image models cannot be trained with diffusion
The flower dataset has no images
questions.answer: Training one that works well is expensive and time consuming
questions.explanation: The book says you have all the ingredients, but training a good text-to-image diffusion model is quite expensive and slow. Keras can express it (option 1 is false), diffusion is exactly the method (option 3 is false), and option 4 is nonsense.

questions.question: In Listing 17.8, what does image_shape=(height, width, 3) with height, width = 512, 512 control?
questions.answer: The resolution and channel count of the generated images: 512×512 RGB.
questions.explanation: image_shape configures the task's output size. In Listing 17.9 the latent noise is sized height // 8 by width // 8 accordingly.

questions.question: Can you explain, in your own words, how you would modify the DiffusionModel from section 17.2 to accept a text prompt? Which parts of the code would change and which would stay the same?
questions.answer: Change: the dataset (yield (prompt, image) pairs), a frozen text encoder to embed prompts, and the denoiser architecture (an extra text_embeddings input injected into the network). Same: noise sampling, diffusion schedule, loss on predicted noise, and the iterative generation loop (with the prompt embedding passed at every step).
questions.explanation: Follows the page's description: same diffusion process, extra input to the denoiser, training on (prompt, image) pairs.
